classification.difficultyReason: Order six observations and average the two middle values, repeated directly for three lists.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess calculating a median. Each dataset has six values, so the third and fourth ordered values are averaged. The supplied mean is retained but is unnecessary for this calculation.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 explains ordering values and averaging the two middle values for an even-sized dataset. Page 3 Example 2 demonstrates this method with ten heights. The printed margin reference for question 1 is Example 3; that example calculates a mean, while Example 2 supplies the relevant median method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Orders six values and averages the two middle values in each dataset.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply familiar even-count median and arithmetic mean procedures and round to the specified two decimals.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess calculation of measures of centre using these demonstrated procedures. The source margin reference to Examples 2 and 3 is retained as editable text.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines mean as the sum divided by the number of values. Page 3 Example 2 orders the data and averages the two middle values; Example 3 substitutes all measurements into the mean formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly applies the taught median and mean procedures to twelve measurements.

classification.difficultyReason: Invert the taught mean definition to recover a count from the supplied mean and total.

questions.mappingNote: find-value-from-mean is the closest existing skill because the unknown quantity is recovered from a supplied total and mean. The offered potato-price reuse candidate has a different mean, $4.50 rather than $7.50, so this question is authored independently.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines the mean as the sum of the values divided by the number of values. Pages 2–3 demonstrate substitution into this formula. Recovering the count here uses ordinary inverse operations on that same formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses a supplied mean and total to determine the number of observations.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate two measures and explain the effect of an extreme observation on contextual typical spending.

questions.mappingNote: Choosing and justifying the more representative measure in part c is the most advanced directly assessed skill; parts a and b apply the taught median and mean calculations.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 define the mean as total divided by count and find an even-sized dataset’s median by ordering the values and averaging the two central values. Example 4 on page 4 calculates mean and median for prices with extreme high values. Pages 3 and 6 explain that extreme values affect the mean and can make the median a better indication of typical spending.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate two measures of centre and explain why an unusually expensive lunch makes the median more representative.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct ten-entry lists subject to value bounds and a supplied mean, recognising endpoint necessity and checking an interior sample.

questions.mappingNote: find-value-from-mean is the closest existing skill because students select data values to achieve a supplied mean. The question assesses construction as well as calculation, rather than comparison of datasets.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines the mean as the sum divided by the number of values; pages 2–5 demonstrate substitution into that formula. Constructing constant ten-entry lists and checking their means directly uses this taught method. The bounds 1 and 3 establish why the endpoint cases require constant lists; no additional dataset-construction technique is needed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Constructs ten-entry datasets satisfying a specified mean and restricted possible values.

classification.difficultyReason: Decode a stem-and-leaf representation and then apply familiar mean and median procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Calculating mean and median from the represented observations directly matches calculate-mean-median-mode-range.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 define the mean and the median of ordered data. Pages 4–5 explain stems and leaves; Example 6 demonstrates calculating the mean and averaging the two middle observations from a stem-and-leaf plot. The solution applies these methods to the question's own data, independently of the erroneous numerator printed in Example 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reads twenty observations from a stem-and-leaf plot and calculates their mean and median.

classification.difficultyReason: Decode a complete dataset, compute both measures, then filter boundary observations and recompute with the changed count and median parity.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly apply these demonstrated methods to the supplied integer stem-and-leaf data.
questions.methodNote: Use the ordered middle observation for an odd count, average the middle pair for an even count, and divide the sum by the count. Example 4 demonstrates excluding extreme observations; Examples 5 and 6 demonstrate interpreting integer stems and leaves.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read a stem-and-leaf plot and recalculate both measures after excluding extreme observations.

classification.difficultyReason: Compute measures of centre and justify the more representative measure in the presence of unusually large observations.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the mean formula and odd-count median method on page 2, supported by the calculations on pages 3–5. Part b directly applies the house-price discussion and Example 4 on pages 3–4 and the comparison of measures on page 6.
questions.methodNote: Find the mean by dividing the sum by the number of values. Order the data and select the middle value for an odd-sized dataset. Prefer the median when unusually large values distort the mean.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate two measures of centre and justify the more representative measure for unevenly distributed suburb areas.

classification.difficultyReason: Organise decimal data using a place-value stem and explicit key, then calculate two measures of centre.

questions.mappingNote: Part a assesses representation with a stem-and-leaf plot; parts b and c directly apply the taught median and mean procedures. The decimal place-value extension in part a requires independent method reconciliation.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 teach averaging all values and averaging the two middle ordered values. Pages 4–5 teach stem-and-leaf construction with ordered leaves and a key, using integer observations. Decimal stems/leaves are not explicitly demonstrated.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Organise decimal measurements into a stem-and-leaf plot and calculate their median and mean.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct several distinct positive integer datasets under simultaneous mean and median constraints, organise middle-value restrictions and verify every candidate.

questions.mappingNote: The solutions use the taught mean definition to obtain totals of 12 and 15, and the taught median rules to constrain the ordered middle values. Constructing candidate lists and checking both conditions applies these definitions directly, without introducing an algebraic shortcut or a new representation.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 define the mean as total divided by count and distinguish the odd-count middle value from the even-count average of the two middle values. Pages 4–6 reinforce these calculations. No worked dataset-construction example is supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct several distinct positive whole-number datasets satisfying simultaneous mean and median constraints.

classification.difficultyReason: Count the supplied categories, construct separate columns and convert counts to proportions and percentages using the given sample size; these are familiar linked representations.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 directly applies the categorical-marble model and relative-frequency formula on page 10 to a new list of 20 observations.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 models counting categorical observations, drawing separate columns and dividing each frequency by the dataset size before expressing the result as a percentage. Page 11 discusses sample proportions. Pages 2–3 concern means and medians and supply no additional method needed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count three categories, construct a column graph and express the counts as fractions and percentages of 20.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide each of three supplied category counts by the supplied total20; no modelling choice or additional inference.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses expressing each category count as a fraction of the sample total, matching quantity-as-fraction-percentage.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 defines relative frequency as frequency divided by dataset size and demonstrates category proportions for a sample of 20. Page 11 discusses sample proportions; pages 2–3 concern means and medians.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide each supplied category frequency by the stated sample size.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate two supplied-sample means, select the ten extreme observations from the full list and calculate their means; linked sorting and mean procedures are familiar.

questions.mappingNote: Each response directly assesses calculating a mean. Parts b and c first require ordering the supplied observations and selecting ten values, including repeated masses.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 calculate the mean by adding all observations and dividing by their count. Page 11 applies means to numerical samples and discusses their variability; page 10 supplies the preceding categorical-sampling context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate sample means and select the ten smallest and ten largest observations before averaging.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent supplied categorical counts as a column graph, total the counts and calculate relative frequencies; straightforward linked statistical procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the categorical column-graph model; part b applies the relative-frequency formula to the four supplied sample counts. The closest primary skill is expressing a quantity as a fraction of the sample total.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 models categorical column graphs and defines relative frequency as frequency divided by dataset size. Page 11 explains sample proportions. Pages 2–3 concern means and medians and do not supply a different method for this question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a categorical column graph from a supplied table and divide each frequency by the sample total.

classification.difficultyReason: Add the ten given lengths and divide by their stated count; a direct mean calculation.

questions.mappingNote: The frog measurements are numerical sample data; the directly assessed operation is calculating their mean.
questions.methodNote: Add the sample measurements and divide by the number of measurements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a sample mean from ten supplied measurements.

classification.difficultyReason: Select extreme subsets for the means, then recognise the unprompted integrality obstruction to a proposed mean rather than searching examples; the impossibility justification is the hardest essential demand.

questions.mappingNote: Part a compares possible sample means; part b uses the required sample sum to establish impossibility.
questions.methodNote: Calculate each sample mean as its sum divided by its size; reverse that calculation to test a proposed mean.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select extremal samples and explain why a specified mean is impossible.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert five supplied counts to percentages with specified precision and construct their frequency graph; linked familiar representations with no method selection.

questions.mappingNote: The question combines relative-frequency calculations and categorical graph construction. The answer-key graph establishes count frequencies as the intended representation in part b.
questions.methodNote: Relative frequency is frequency divided by dataset size; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Represent categorical counts using separated columns.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert counts into percentages and represent categorical counts with a scaled column graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Carry out the prescribed replacement sampling procedure, calculate a proportion and compare repeated estimates; the investigation supplies the sampling model and calculation target.

questions.mappingNote: Replacement, mixing, sample size and comparison are explicitly assessed practical requirements.
questions.methodNote: Estimate a population proportion using sample relative frequencies and compare the variability of repeated sample results.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Conduct repeated sampling with replacement and compare estimates of a population proportion.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate red proportions from collected samples, choose a consistent dot-plot scale and compare the spread of students' estimates. Supplied population and sampling guidance supports these linked procedures; no unsignposted insight is required.

questions.mappingNote: The practical task asks for red proportions and comparison of students' sample-based estimates.
questions.methodNote: Distinguish population from sample, calculate sample relative frequencies and display variability using a dot plot.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate red proportions from collected samples, choose a consistent dot-plot scale and compare the spread of students' estimates. Supplied population and sampling guidance supports these linked procedures; no unsignposted insight is required.

classification.difficultyReason: Design a question and population within a supplied stepwise survey protocol, pilot it, choose random selection and compare sample proportions; the stages scaffold each familiar decision.

questions.mappingNote: Survey design is the most advanced directly assessed skill across the complete activity. Parts d–f also assess collection, proportions and interpretation of sampling variation.
questions.methodNote: Identify the population, select a random sample, calculate a sample proportion as frequency divided by sample size, and recognise variation between samples.

classification.difficultyReason: Implement equal-chance digit sampling, convert sample even counts to proportions, plot repeated results and compare larger samples using the taught variability model.

questions.mappingNote: The activity directly investigates variation between sample proportions and the effect of sample size. Pages 9–11 provide the relevant relative-frequency and sampling context.
questions.methodNote: Select random samples with equal selection chances; calculate a sample proportion as frequency divided by sample size; compare repeated sample proportions using a dot plot.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect repeated numerical samples, calculate their means and compare dot-plot variability after increasing size, following an explicit practical sequence.

questions.mappingNote: Comparing the distributions of repeated sample means is the most advanced directly assessed task. Collection, mean calculation and dot plotting support that comparison.
questions.methodNote: Calculate each sample mean by adding its numerical values and dividing by the sample size. Represent repeated results with a dot plot. Compare variability for samples of different sizes, following the sample-means examples on page 11.

bankProjection.note: Source-confirmed category headings are omitted only from bank prompts and presentation. Explicit equivalent fraction notation repairs satisfy bank validation. Source booklet content and all questions are retained.
